transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-13 15:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Recording: FF-link-not-provided

Summary: planning conversation for an on-prem sealed deployment of Redwood Private in Aurora's locked research vault. Lots of questions about offline updates, signed artifacts, and hardware limits.

[00:00:03] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Really excited to talk through the locked network setup and what we can actually deliver on-prem. Quick intros?
[00:00:14] Dr. Lena (Aurora CTO): Hi, I'm Lena. We're the CTO, running a lot of the genomics pipelines. We have strict isolation requirements for patient data and compute.
[00:00:20] Samir (MLOps): Samir here, I run the MLOps team and will own the POC.
[00:00:24] Olivia (InfoSec): Olivia, InfoSec. I'll be vetting any update mechanisms and attestations.
[00:00:28] Jae (Infra): And Jae, infra engineer. I'll be your contact for racks and networking.
[00:00:32] Dmitri (Redwood SE): Dmitri from Redwood, I'll dig into the runtime and the image signing flow.
[00:00:36] Maya: Great. High level: Aurora is evaluating Hosted, Dedicated, or Private. It sounds like Private on-prem in a locked network is where you're headed. Can you walk us through the constraints?
[00:00:47] Jae: Sure. The site is an isolated data center — no egress to the internet. We have an operations jump-host in a DMZ that can be used for push updates via physically-approved media. USB is allowed in encrypted YubiKey-like device form factor, but we have a strict chain-of-custody for any removable media.
[00:01:05] Olivia: Right, and we require signed artifacts and cryptographic verification, ideally integrated with an HSM in our security vault. We also need audit trails that we can export for SOC2/ISO auditors.
[00:01:14] Maya: Okay, that's helpful. Dmitri, are we OK supporting an offline update flow where images are signed by Redwood and then verified by the customer's HSM on site?
[00:01:22] Dmitri: Yes, we have a pattern for signed image bundles. The typical flow we propose is: Redwood produces a signed bundle, we deliver the bundle over physical media, Aurora verifies the bundle signature against a public key both stored in the HSM and a local trust store, then the deployment agent applies the update. There are a few variants depending on whether you want Redwood's private key to sign or a mutual signing approach.
[00:01:46] Olivia: A mutual signing model is preferable — Aurora's HSM should vouch for the deployer and we should be able to produce a signed attestation back to Redwood for supportability without exposing keys.
[00:01:57] Dmitri: Totally, that's doable. We'll want to define the attestation format — typically a TPM-backed signature or an HSM-signed SAML/JSON Web Token that says 'image applied at timestamp X, node IDs Y'.
[00:02:09] Samir: What's the mechanism for rollback if we find a regressor? We can't have months of downtime.
[00:02:13] Dmitri: We support atomic switchovers with image version pinning. On an air-gapped site you would keep previous images on local NVMe and our orchestrator handles fast rollback. The key there is ensuring enough NVMe to hold two or three image generations.
[00:02:27] Jae: Note: our chassis are dense — 2U nodes with two GPUs each, no NVLink interconnect. PCIe lanes are at a premium and we can't add extra NVMe without custom trays. Cooling is also tight. What's Redwood's recommendation for GPU choice? H100 vs A100, quantized vs full FP16?
[00:02:43] Dmitri: For genomics inference workloads with long contexts, H100 will give you better memory bandwidth and sparsity gains. But if cost and power are constraints, an A100 80GB in INT8/4-bit quant mode with KV cache offload to NVMe can be viable. We can provide a config with throughput estimates for both.
[00:03:01] Maya: We'll include that in the follow-up. Also, Jae, given limited NVMe, we can recommend a caching strategy — smaller KV cache per node and more aggressive prefix caching at the application layer — to reduce per-token memory pressure.
[00:03:12] Samir: How about model updates? Are we swapping model files or pushing a container with the model baked in?
[00:03:17] Dmitri: We tend to ship signed model artifacts (model.tar.gz) and a lightweight runtime container. In air-gapped setups, customers often prefer to validate and sign the runtime container locally as well. For auditability, we store the image digest and the provenance metadata in the attestation.
[00:03:34] Olivia: We need to be able to show chain-of-custody — who brought the media, who signed it, verification steps. Also retention for logs for at least three years for some of our regulated projects.
[00:03:44] Maya: Redwood Console's observability can export token-level traces, per-request latencies, and operation logs; in Private we can ship a log collector that writes to your SIEM. On an air-gapped site, that's a push/pull ledger pattern where the collector writes to a local archive and you provide read access for auditors.
[00:03:59] Samir: Is the collector agent a separate binary, or is it integrated into the runtime?
[00:04:03] Dmitri: It's a separate agent that communicates with the runtime over a localhost socket; that makes it easy to quarantine or disable if necessary.
[00:04:08] Jae: We also have questions about licensing and counting. If we go with Reserved nodes, do you do per-GPU licensing, or per-server?
[00:04:15] Maya: Dedicated/reserved is typically capacity-based (vCPU/GPU pools) with contractual commits. For on-prem Private, we do a node-based license tied to the customer deployment; details vary if you want a consumption-like meter vs a fixed appliance fee. We'll send examples.
[00:04:29] Dr. Lena: Timeline question: we have a regulatory review window in Q1. Ideally we'd have a POC in December and full onboarding by February. Is that realistic?
[00:04:38] Dmitri: If you can provide hardware inventory and a sealed rack or lab for testing, a focused POC in 4–6 weeks is possible. The gating factor is image signing and your audit acceptance.
[00:04:48] Samir: POC success criteria — low latency for small prompt sets, model parity with hosted baseline, ability to do offline updates with verified signatures, and generation throughput targets.
[00:04:57] Maya: Good list. We'll capture that as the POC criteria and circulate.
[00:05:01] [00:05:10] Olivia (interrupt): One technical deep question: can Redwood's runtime run without privileged container capabilities? We run strict PodSecurityPolicy-like constraints and in our environment we disallow CAP_SYS_ADMIN.
[00:05:20] Dmitri: The runtime needs some capabilities for device access to GPUs — usually we ask for node-level permissions to access /dev/nvidia* or to use an NVIDIA device plugin. But we've run in environments with very limited kernel capabilities by using a driverless mode and mediated device plugins. It's more complex but feasible.
[00:05:40] Jae: So that means we may have to provision specific driver versions. Our cluster uses a custom kernel for compliance. How brittle is the runtime across kernel versions?
[00:05:49] Dmitri: We test against a matrix of common kernels, but custom kernels can surface edge cases. We recommend providing a staging node to validate drivers. We can also provide a certified OS image for the sealed lab to reduce surprises.
[00:06:03] Samir: Any limitations on model size? We run some really large Transformer variants for variant calling, 40B-ish.
[00:06:10] Dmitri: 40B models are feasible but will push memory and NVMe offload. For strict latency SLOs you want H100 or a sharded multi-GPU approach. Model parallelism across nodes adds network complexity; given your locked network, that can still work but you need a high-speed private fabric.
[00:06:24] Dr. Lena: Our network fabric is 100GbE with RDMA disabled for security. Will that be an issue?
[00:06:29] Dmitri: RDMA helps for model sharding but isn't strictly required. If you can't use RDMA, we'll benchmark on 100GbE and may recommend fewer but beefier GPUs per node to avoid inter-node sharding latency.
[00:06:41] Maya: Switching gears to support model updates and regressions: Aurora wants the ability to run evals locally against a golden prompt set and have Redwood alert on regressions even when offline.
[00:06:52] Dmitri: We can ship an eval runner that runs locally and creates a signed report you can choose to share with Redwood. In offline modes you can run the evals, and if you want automated alerts, there's a pull-forward pattern where you push the signed report onto the jump host for Redwood to pick up — with mutual auth.
[00:07:06] Olivia: Will Redwood store any payloads from us in your hosted environment if we send signed reports? We have strict data residency rules.
[00:07:13] Maya: We can negotiate a minimal metadata-only exchange — for example, hashes and pass/fail signals. If you don't want any data leaving the site, we can work with a support-only model where you send logs through your portal and our support references the signed attestations to advise.
[00:07:27] [00:07:35] Jae: Physical process question — chain-of-custody for media: our security team wants to see step-by-step: who signs, who transports, who hand-delivers, who verifies. Can Redwood provide a standard operating procedure?
[00:07:46] Dmitri: Yes, we have an SOP template for sealed deliveries and chain-of-custody. It covers signing policy, key rotation cadence, checksums, and verification steps on the target host. We'll tailor it to your HSM vendor (you mentioned Utimaco? or Gemalto?)
[00:07:58] Olivia: We're using Thales/Idemia HSMs in the security vault.
[00:08:02] Dmitri: Great, we can map the signing and verification commands to Thales APIs and provide sample scripts.
[00:08:06] Samir: On the operational side, if we find a bug that requires a patch, what's the fastest way to get a hotfix into the locked lab? We can't wait for a quarterly maintenance window sometimes.
[00:08:16] Maya: We support an expedited sealed-media emergency flow. It requires prior approvals and a two-party signature: Redwood signs the fix, Aurora's on-site security signs receipt, and the HSM records an attestation. That reduces lead time but still maintains auditability.
[00:08:31] Dr. Lena: Good. Can you give a sample SLA for on-prem like that?
[00:08:35] Maya: We'll include an example SLA in the runbook; note emergency SLAs for air-gapped sites have different constraints and typically cost more because a human must handle media transfers.
[00:08:44] [00:08:52] Dmitri: A few technical caveats I want to call out: 1) We do not recommend using consumer USB keys as the only trust anchor — use HSM-backed keys. 2) If you want reproducible builds we can provide a binary provenance layout with signed SBOMs. 3) Testing images should be signed with a separate test key to avoid accidental promotion.
[00:09:10] Olivia: SBOMs are a must. Also, can Redwood produce a cryptographic log for every update applied? Our auditors ask for a tamper-evident ledger.
[00:09:19] Dmitri: Yes, we can emit a signed ledger entry per update that you store in your local append-only archive. If you want, we can help map that to your SIEM.
[00:09:27] Samir: Let's talk cost a little bit — what are the ballpark numbers for 4-node H100 vs 8-node A100 setups for a POC?
[00:09:35] Maya: I'll send a cost comparison — ballpark, H100 hardware/capex is higher but perf-per-Watt and perf-per-dollar at scale might favor H100 for heavy inference. We'll attach our benchmarking spreadsheet and a sample bill-of-materials.
[00:09:48] [00:09:55] Dr. Lena: Anything else on the security checklist?
[00:09:58] Olivia: SSO — can you integrate with our SAML provider for user auth in the Console when it's air-gapped? We want RBAC mapped to internal groups.
[00:10:06] Dmitri: Yes, we can ship a local SAML IdP connector that validates against a locally-hosted SAML endpoint. Single sign-on without external internet is supported; it's just a config to point to your local IdP.
[00:10:18] Maya: Wrap-up time — to recap: Redwood will send an air-gapped deployment runbook, image signing design, GPU configuration recommendations, and an example SLA. Aurora will share hardware and network diagrams, approved media policy, and the POC criteria. We also want to schedule the technical deep dive to lock down HSM integration.
[00:10:34] Dr. Lena: Sounds good. Any blockers we didn't cover?
[00:10:37] Jae: One small note: our facility's elevator can only handle crates under 60kg. If you need to send physical appliances, factor that in.
[00:10:44] Maya: Noted — logistics matter.
[00:10:47] [00:10:52] Olivia: One last thing — for audits, we need to be able to run a 'forensic snapshot' if required. Can Redwood enable a read-only snapshot export of the last 90 days of logs that we can sign and keep?
[00:11:02] Dmitri: Yes, the collector can produce a forensics bundle with checksums and signed manifests. We'll include the process in the runbook.
[00:11:10] Maya: Excellent. We'll follow up with the docs and propose times for the deep dive. Thanks, everyone.
[00:11:16] Dr. Lena: Thanks all.
[00:11:19] [End of meeting — remaining ~44 minutes not fully transcribed in this export due to recording cutoff; meeting notes continue in action items and follow-ups.]

Notes on transcription quality: speaker overlap clipped in places; a few product names were auto-transcribed (e.g., 'KV cache' as 'K V cash'), and some HSM vendor names mistranscribed initially.
